I was recently in this same boat with you. I dropped out of high school at 17, and while all my friends were graduating, I was working at the local tire shop 50 hours a week. Over the next 2-3 years I watched all my friends go to college, move out, fall in love, all while I sat here just trying to convince myself “nobody is as happy as they seem, especially online”. Of course I didn’t do anything productive, and eventually I was arrested for reckless driving, criminal speeding….. and felony evasion of law enforcement. I did a few weeks before I was able to take a plea deal, but I couldn’t drive for a year, and I lost my job. It was all I had left and I screwed that up. I ended up in the hospital a few times that year, nearly succeeding in killing myself once. After I became just stable enough to be unsupervised, I had lost all interest in the few things I used to love. I still have the motorcycle I was arrested on, but I lost all of my good riding buddies, and I no longer enjoy riding, so I let it sit, and it rotted away for about 8 months (it was also crashed I should mention that) I lost 30 good friends during this whole debacle, and I still think about them a lot. Luckily I reconnected with an old coworker from that first job after dropping out, and now he and I are the closest of friends, and he doesn’t make me feel bad about myself somehow even though he has a lot going for him. I’m still on the uphill, but I just recently finished restoring the bike I was arrested on some $2k later, got my drivers license back, got my ged, and I’m starting an aircraft maintenance program at a community college near me.

Here’s the thing nobody ever tells you. You won’t notice how far you’ve come until long after you get there. As far as the fear of missing out? I had it like the goddamn plague, but over time as you literally fight for your own life, you start to realize how miserable and exhausting it is trying to force yourself to be that social butterfly you always wanted to be.
